companies.description: Designs GPUs and AI chips that power most large-scale AI training and data centers.

company_story.label: What it does
company_story.answer: NVIDIA designs GPUs and AI accelerator chips (plus the CUDA software stack and networking gear) and sells them to companies that build and run AI systems, essentially selling the "picks and shovels" of the AI computing buildout rather than running AI applications itself.

company_story.label: Who its customers are
company_story.answer: Its customers are cloud providers (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Oracle), AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic), large enterprises building AI infrastructure, and to a lesser extent gaming PC makers and automotive/robotics companies.

company_story.label: Competitive edge
company_story.answer: The moat is the combination of raw chip performance, the CUDA software ecosystem that developers have built on for over a decade, and full-stack integration (chips, networking, systems, software) that makes switching to competitors costly and technically risky.

company_story.label: Leadership
company_story.answer: Jensen Huang, co-founder and CEO since 1993, still leads the company — this is from general knowledge and could be out of date if there's been a very recent change.

company_story.answer: Growth potential is tied to continued buildout of AI data center infrastructure, expansion into new markets like robotics, autonomous vehicles, and enterprise AI software, and international demand, though the pace of the last few years' growth is unlikely to be sustained indefinitely.

company_story.label: Risks
company_story.answer: Key risks include customer concentration (a handful of hyperscalers drive a large share of revenue), competition from custom chips built by those same customers (Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium), export restrictions on China sales, potential AI capital spending slowdown, and the recent sharp increase in debt whose purpose isn't yet clear.
